preamble: Merger of the emphatic interdental with the emphatic sibilant: Proto-Semitic *ṯ̣, reconstructed as an ejective dental fricative [θʼ], fell together with *ṣ, reconstructed as the ejective affricate [tsʼ], in Akkadian, Canaanite (Hebrew, Phoenician) and Geʽez: Hebrew ṣēl 'shadow', Akkadian ṣillum, Geʽez ጽላሎት, against Arabic ẓill and Ugaritic ẓillu, which keep a separate interdental, and Aramaic ṭullā, which merged it with ṭ. Wikipedia's Geʽez consonant table gives ጸ as /tsʼ/, and Geʽez sometimes writes these words with ፀ instead (ዐፅም beside ዐጽም 'bone'), a difference that Militarev (2006, no. 2012) says may be purely orthographic or an attempt to render *ṯ̣. That Hebrew and Akkadian ṣ was still an affricate rests on transcriptions (Kogan 2011, cited by Wikipedia). The Proto-Semitic value is a reconstruction: whether the emphatics were ejective or pharyngealized is debated, since the daughter languages differ (pharyngealized in Arabic, Aramaic and Tiberian Hebrew, glottalized in Ethiopian Semitic and Modern South Arabian), though they are generally reconstructed as glottalized, i.e. ejective (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, as cited by Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language), but some reconstructions give *ṯ̣ a pharyngealized value [θˤ] or [ðˤ] (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ), and 'maximal' affricate accounts make it [tθʼ]. This entry follows the [θʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table. Arabic ẓāʾ [ðˤ] and the Modern South Arabian reflex [θʼ ~ ðˤ] have no symbol in the atlas.
